name: Debugging
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Find bugs systematically: read stack traces, use logs and debuggers, know the common bug families, bisect, and ask for help well.

lesson.intro: Developers spend a large share of their time figuring out why code does not do what they expected. The difference between a day lost and a bug fixed before lunch is rarely genius; it is method. This lesson gives you a repeatable process, the tools to see inside a running program, the bug families you will meet again and again, and how to ask for help in a way that gets answers.
objectives: Debug with a repeatable loop: reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, test, fix, prevent
Read Python and JavaScript stack traces to find the failing line in your own code
Choose between print, logging and a debugger, and use pdb and breakpoints
Recognize off-by-one, None, shared state, async, floating point and encoding bugs from their symptoms
Use git bisect, write regression tests, and write bug reports that get fast answers

sections.title: A method: reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, test, fix, prevent
sections.body:
Monday, 10 am. A ticket says: "Some customers see the wrong total at checkout." The tempting move is to open `checkout.py`, spot something that looks odd, change it and push. That is **shotgun debugging**: changing things until the symptom goes away. It is slow, it often hides the bug instead of fixing it, and it can add new ones.

Experienced engineers follow a loop that looks a lot like the scientific method:

- **Reproduce.** Make the bug happen on demand, on your machine. Get the exact input, account, data, browser or version. A bug you can trigger in ten seconds is half fixed; a bug you cannot reproduce can never be shown to be fixed.
- **Isolate.** Shrink the problem. Which customers? Only carts with a coupon? Only since Tuesday's deploy? Remove everything that does not matter until you have the smallest input that still fails.
- **Hypothesize.** Form one specific, testable guess: "the coupon is applied again every time the cart is recalculated".
- **Test the hypothesis.** Design a check that could prove it wrong: a print, a breakpoint, a unit test with that exact input. If the evidence disagrees, drop the guess and form a new one.
- **Fix** the cause, not the symptom. Clamping a negative total to zero makes the complaint go away while the double-applied coupon keeps producing wrong totals that happen to be positive.
- **Prevent.** Add a regression test that fails without your fix, and ask whether the same mistake lives anywhere else.

Habits that make the loop fast:

- **Change one thing at a time**, and undo changes that did not help.
- **Read the whole error message** before doing anything else.
- **Question your assumptions.** "That function can't return None" is what people say right before discovering that it does. Check instead of assuming.
- **Keep notes** of what you tried and what you saw. They stop you going in circles, and they become your bug report if you need help.
- **Ask what changed.** A bug that appeared suddenly usually came from a recent deploy, dependency upgrade, configuration change or new kind of data.
sections.code:
BUG: wrong checkout total for some customers (ticket SHOP-311)

Reproduce:   user 5521, cart [mug 12.00, shirt 20.00], coupon SPRING10
             expected 28.80, got 25.92                  (every time)
Isolate:     no coupon -> correct.  Fixed-amount coupons -> correct.
             Only percentage coupons, only after the cart is edited.
Hypothesis:  the discount is applied again on each recalculation
Test:        unit test: apply SPRING10, recalculate twice -> 25.92  (confirmed)
Fix:         recalculate() starts from the undiscounted subtotal
Prevent:     regression test test_recalculating_cart_keeps_single_discount
sections.pitfall: Changing several things at once and watching the bug disappear. You do not know which change fixed it, or whether one of the others broke something else. One change, one observation.

check.question: A user reports a crash that you cannot trigger on your machine. What is the most useful next step?
choices: Wrap the suspected function in try/except so it cannot crash
Get the exact input, account, version and steps, and keep trying to reproduce it
Rewrite the module, since the bug is hard to find
Close the ticket as cannot reproduce
check.explanation: Without a reproduction you cannot test a hypothesis or prove a fix. The difference between their run and yours (data, version, browser, settings) is usually the clue itself. Catching the error blindly only hides it.

sections.title: Reading stack traces in Python and JavaScript
sections.body:
An error with a stack trace is the program telling you exactly where it was and what it was doing when it failed. Newcomers often panic at the wall of text, or paste only the last line into a search engine. Reading it carefully is usually faster than either.

**Python tracebacks** begin with `Traceback (most recent call last):`. The frames are listed oldest call first, so the most recent call, where the error was raised, is at the **bottom**. Read them bottom-up:

- The **last line** is the exception type and message: `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`. Read all of it.
- The **frame just above it** is the line that raised the error, with file, line number and function name.
- Keep going up to the **first frame in your own code**. Frames inside third-party libraries or the standard library are rarely where the bug is; the bug is usually in how your code called them.
- The `~~~^^^` markers (Python 3.11 and later) underline the exact expression that failed on that line.

Two phrases to recognize in longer tracebacks. "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred" means a second error happened inside an `except` block. "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" means the code used `raise ... from err`. Either way, the root cause is in the **first** traceback printed.

**JavaScript stack traces** run the other way. The error type and message come first, then the `at ...` lines with the **most recent call first**, so the top `at` line is where it failed, as `file:line:column`. Node also prints the offending source line with a caret under the exact spot. Frames that start with `node:internal` are Node's own machinery, so skip them. In the browser, the DevTools console shows the same stack with clickable links, mapped back to your original source through source maps when you use a bundler.

Then ask the right question. In the Python example, the trace says `len(orders)` was zero. The bug is not the division; it is that `build_report` never considered a customer with no orders. A stack trace shows **where** the program noticed a problem. Your job is to work out **why** the values were what they were.
sections.code:
$ python report.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/report.py", line 10, in <module>
    print(build_report(1042))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^
  File "/app/report.py", line 8, in build_report
    return {"customer": customer_id, "aov": average_order_value(orders)}
                                            ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "/app/orders.py", line 3, in average_order_value     <- raised here
    return total / len(orders)
           ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero                          <- read first

$ node receipts.js
/app/receipts.js:9
  const to = customer.email
                      ^

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')
    at sendReceipt (/app/receipts.js:9:23)                  <- failed here
    at Object.<anonymous> (/app/receipts.js:13:1)
    at Module._compile (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1706:14)
sections.pitfall: Searching for the last line only and pasting the first fix you find. The message says what went wrong, the frames say where in your code. Read both before changing anything.

activity.title: Read the traceback, then fix
activity.prompt: Run it and read the traceback bottom-up: the message says how many values were expected and how many arrived, and the frames show which function and line. Work out which input line caused it, then fix order_total so it skips blank lines. Do not touch the stapler line: `int(" 1 ")` already copes with spaces.

check.question: In a Python traceback, where is the line that actually raised the exception?
choices: At the top, right after "Traceback (most recent call last):"
In the middle, in the longest frame
At the bottom, just above the exception message
It is not shown; only the calling line is
check.explanation: Python lists the most recent call last, so the frame that raised the error sits directly above the final exception line. JavaScript does the opposite and puts the failing frame first.

sections.title: Print, logging and the debugger
sections.body:
You have a hypothesis. Now you need to see what the program is actually doing. There are three tools, and good engineers use all three.

**Print debugging** is fast and works everywhere. `print(f"{cart_id=} {total=}")` prints names and values (the `=` inside an f-string does that), and `console.log({ cartId, total })` does the same in JavaScript. It is perfect for a quick look. It gets messy when you need many of them, and leftover prints sneak into pull requests, so delete them before you commit.

**Logging** is print debugging that stays in the code on purpose. A logging library adds timestamps, severity levels and the module name, and lets you turn detail up or down without editing code:

- Levels from least to most severe: `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, `CRITICAL`. A logger only emits messages at or above its configured level, and Python's default is `WARNING`. That is why `logger.info(...)` lines seem to vanish until you configure logging.
- Create one logger per module with `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`.
- Pass values as arguments, as in `logger.info("charged order %s", order_id)`, so the string is only built if the message is emitted.
- Inside an `except` block, `logger.exception("...")` logs at ERROR level and includes the traceback.
- Log the context future you will need: request id, user id, order id. Never log passwords, tokens or full card numbers.

In production, logs are often the only evidence you get, so good logging is part of building a feature, not an afterthought.

**A debugger** pauses the running program so you can inspect everything at that moment. In Python, put `breakpoint()` on a line (or run `python -m pdb script.py`) and use the `(Pdb)` prompt:

- `n` (next) runs the current line and stops at the next one; `s` (step) goes into the function called on this line.
- `c` (continue) runs until the next breakpoint; `p expr` prints any expression, such as `p order.items`.
- `l` lists the code around you, `w` (where) shows the call stack, and `q` quits.

In JavaScript, a `debugger;` statement pauses when DevTools is open, and `node --inspect` lets Chrome DevTools or VS Code attach to Node. Editors let you click in the gutter to set breakpoints, add **conditional breakpoints** (pause only when `order.id === 7`), watch expressions, and walk up the call stack to see each caller's variables. A debugger shines when you do not yet know what to print, or when the state is large and nested.

Rule of thumb: print for a quick look, logging for anything you may need again (especially in production), and the debugger when you need to explore.
sections.code:
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def apply_coupon(cart, code):
    logger.debug("applying coupon %s to cart %s", code, cart.id)
    coupon = find_coupon(code)
    if coupon is None:
        logger.info("unknown coupon %s for cart %s", code, cart.id)
        return cart
    breakpoint()          # pauses here: try  p cart.total_cents  then  n
    cart.total_cents -= cart.total_cents * coupon.percent // 100
    return cart


# Once, at startup:
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.DEBUG,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
sections.pitfall: Committing a leftover `breakpoint()`, `debugger;` or noisy print. A stray `breakpoint()` makes a server hang, waiting for input that never comes. Read your own diff before pushing; many teams add a lint rule for it.

check.question: A payment failed in production last night and you need to know why this morning. Which tool can actually help?
choices: A breakpoint() added to the payment code now
Print statements added to the code now
Rubber duck debugging
Log lines with context, such as the order id, written when it happened
check.explanation: Prints and breakpoints only help for runs that happen after you add them, and you cannot pause production. Logs written at the time are the evidence, which is why logging context is part of building features.

sections.title: Bug families: off-by-one, None and shared state
sections.body:
Most bugs you meet belong to a handful of families. Recognizing the family from the symptom gets you to the cause much faster.

**Off-by-one errors.** A loop runs one time too many or too few, or a range includes or excludes an end it should not. Symptoms: the first or last item is missing or doubled, `IndexError: list index out of range`, a page showing 9 results instead of 10. Usual suspects: `range(1, n)` when you meant `range(n)`, `<=` versus `<`, using `len(items)` as an index (the last index is `len(items) - 1`), and forgetting that slice and range ends are exclusive. Check the edges explicitly: the first item, the last item and an empty list.

**None and undefined.** Something you expected to be an object is missing. In Python it reads `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'email'` or `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`; in JavaScript, `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The crashing line is rarely the bug. Ask where the value came from: a lookup that found nothing (`dict.get`, `Map.get`, `find()`, a database query), a function that forgot to `return` (Python then returns `None`), a misspelled key, an id that is a string in one place and a number in another, or an API response missing a field. Then decide what should happen when it is missing and handle that on purpose: a guard clause, a clear error, or optional chaining (`customer?.email`) when absence is genuinely fine.

**Shared mutable state.** Two parts of the program hold the same object, and one changes it under the other. Classic forms:

- **Aliasing:** `b = a` does not copy a list or dict; both names point at one object. `[[]] * 3` builds a list holding the **same** inner list three times.
- **Mutable default arguments:** `def f(items=[])` shares one list across every call.
- **Module-level state** such as a global cache or a class attribute list, shared by every caller and every test.

Symptoms: values change "by themselves", one user's data appears for another, tests pass alone and fail together. Fix it by copying on purpose (`list(a)`, `dict(a)`, or `copy.deepcopy(a)` for nested data), creating fresh objects (`[[] for _ in range(3)]`), and keeping state local.
sections.code:
# Off-by-one: range(1, ...) skips index 0, the first player
for i in range(1, len(players)):
    ...

# None: dict.get returns None when the key is missing
customer = customers.get(order.customer_id)
send(customer.email)     # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'email'

# Aliasing: one inner list, three references to it
teams = [[]] * 3
teams[0].append("Ana")
print(teams)             # [['Ana'], ['Ana'], ['Ana']]

teams = [[] for _ in range(3)]
teams[0].append("Ana")
print(teams)             # [['Ana'], [], []]
sections.pitfall: Fixing a None crash by wrapping the crashing line in `if customer:`. The order is still processed without a customer; the bug has just moved somewhere quieter. Find out why the value is missing.

activity.title: Two bugs, two families
activity.prompt: This should deal six players into three teams, round robin. Run it: every team has the same five players. There are two bugs from two different families. Fix one, run again, and notice how the output changes before you hunt for the second.

props.task: Make the output: team 1: Ana, Dee / team 2: Ben, Eli / team 3: Cy, Fay (one per line)
props.expectOutput:
team 1: Ana, Dee
team 2: Ben, Eli
team 3: Cy, Fay

check.question: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')` is thrown at `user.name`. Where is the bug most likely to be?
choices: In the property name, because name is reserved in JavaScript
In the line after the crash
Wherever user came from: a lookup, return value or response that produced undefined
In the JavaScript engine's property access
check.explanation: The crash is just where the missing value was first used. Trace user back to its source, such as a find() that matched nothing or an id with the wrong type, and fix it there.

sections.title: Bug families: async timing, floating point, encoding
sections.body:
**Async timing.** Asynchronous code runs later than it looks, and its bugs hide in that gap.

- **A missing `await`.** In JavaScript, calling an async function without `await` returns a pending promise and moves on, so the next line runs before the work is done and any failure becomes an unhandled rejection. In Python, calling an `async def` function without `await` only creates a coroutine object that never runs, and Python warns `RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fetch_price' was never awaited`.
- **`forEach` with an async callback.** `rows.forEach(async (row) => await save(row))` waits for nothing, because forEach ignores the promises its callback returns. Use `for (const row of rows) await save(row)` to go one at a time, or `await Promise.all(rows.map(save))` to run them in parallel.
- **Race conditions.** Two operations overlap and the result depends on which finishes first. Two requests that each read a counter, add one and write it back lose an update; a search box shows results for an old query because that response arrived last. The symptoms are intermittent and often vanish when you add a print, because the print changes the timing. Fix them with proper awaiting, atomic database operations, locks, or by discarding stale responses.

**Floating point.** Most decimals cannot be stored exactly in binary floating point, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` in both Python and JavaScript, and `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is false. Never compare floats with `==`: use a tolerance, such as `math.isclose(a, b)` in Python or `Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9` in JavaScript. For **money**, avoid floats entirely. Store integer cents, or use Python's `Decimal` built from strings (`Decimal("0.10")`), and format only for display.

**Encoding.** Text is stored as bytes, and an encoding (almost always UTF-8 today) maps between the two. Bugs appear when bytes written with one encoding are read with another:

- `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 3: invalid continuation byte` means the file is not UTF-8, often an old Latin-1 or Windows-1252 export.
- **Mojibake**, such as `cafÃ©` instead of `café`, means UTF-8 bytes were decoded as Latin-1 or Windows-1252.

Fixes: pass the encoding explicitly, as in `open(path, encoding="utf-8")`, because Python's default depends on the operating system and is often not UTF-8 on Windows; decode at the edges of the program and work with text inside; and remember that one character can take several bytes (`len("café")` is 4, but its UTF-8 form is 5 bytes).
sections.pitfall: Fixing a timing bug by adding a `sleep` or `setTimeout`. It changes the odds, not the logic, so the bug returns on a slower machine or a busier day. Wait for the actual operation instead.

activity.title: Make the bill add up
activity.prompt: Run it: the total prints as 23.599999999999998 and the bill looks unpaid by a tiny negative amount. Store each price as integer cents (priceCents: 1210 and so on), keep paid in cents too, compare cents with cents, and format only when printing with (cents / 100).toFixed(2).

props.task: Make the output: total: 23.60 then paid in full

check.question: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` evaluate to false in JavaScript?
choices: === compares types, and the sum is a string
JavaScript rounds every sum down to one decimal place
0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary floating-point form, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004
Addition of decimals is not commutative in JavaScript
check.explanation: Both numbers are stored as the nearest binary fraction, and the tiny errors add up to a value just above 0.3. Python behaves the same way. Compare with a tolerance, and use integer cents or decimals for money.

sections.title: When you are stuck: git bisect and the rubber duck
sections.body:
The checkout total was right in release v2.3.0 and is wrong today. Sixty commits from six people landed in between, and reading them all would take hours. **git bisect** finds the commit that introduced the bug by binary search, the same halving trick as searching a sorted array:

- Run `git bisect start`, then `git bisect bad` to mark the current commit as broken and `git bisect good v2.3.0` to mark a known-good one.
- Git checks out a commit halfway between. Test it (run the app or a test) and answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`.
- Each answer halves the range. Sixty commits take about 6 steps; a thousand take about 10.
- Git prints `<hash> is the first bad commit`. Read that commit's diff: the bug is almost always in it.
- `git bisect reset` takes you back to where you started.

If you can write a command that exits 0 when the code is good and non-zero when it is bad, git can run every step for you: `git bisect run pytest tests/test_checkout.py`. An exit code of 125 tells bisect to skip a commit that cannot be tested, for example one that does not build, and so does `git bisect skip` when you are testing by hand. Bisect works best when every commit on `main` builds and passes its tests, which is one more reason teams care about small, green commits.

The same halving idea works without git: comment out half of a function, delete half of an input file, or disable half the plugins, and see which half still fails.

**Rubber duck debugging**, a name popularized by the book *The Pragmatic Programmer*, means explaining your code line by line, out loud, to someone who knows nothing about it, even a rubber duck on your desk. It works because explaining forces you to state every assumption ("and here `items` is always sorted..."), and the false one often jumps out mid-sentence. Writing a careful question for a teammate has the same effect; plenty of bugs get solved halfway through typing the message.

Other ways to get unstuck: take a short walk, compare against something that works (diff the config, the data, the environment), and check that you are running the code you think you are running: right branch, file saved, server restarted, cache cleared.
sections.code:
$ git bisect start
$ git bisect bad                     # the current commit has the bug
$ git bisect good v2.3.0             # this release was fine
Bisecting: 29 revisions left to test after this (roughly 5 steps)
[4f6ba8d19f35b4c93d0ee0efebd26bd0e6325436] Cache tax rates per region
$ pytest tests/test_checkout.py      # test this commit...
$ git bisect good                    # ...and report the result
Bisecting: 14 revisions left to test after this (roughly 4 steps)
...
afe409fc0b67c015cd35350c2fd033b918b615d3 is the first bad commit
commit afe409fc0b67c015cd35350c2fd033b918b615d3
    Round each line item before summing
$ git bisect reset                   # back to where you started

# Or let git drive. Exit code 0 = good, 1 to 127 except 125 = bad, 125 = skip.
$ git bisect run pytest tests/test_checkout.py
sections.pitfall: Marking a commit bad because of a different, unrelated failure, such as a build error. That sends bisect down the wrong half. Use `git bisect skip` for commits you cannot test.

check.question: About 1,000 commits separate a known-good release from today's broken main. Roughly how many commits will git bisect ask you to test?
choices: About 500
About 10
About 100
check.explanation: Each answer halves the remaining range, so it takes about log2(1000), roughly 10 steps. That is why bisect beats reading commits one by one as soon as there are more than a handful.

sections.title: Regression tests and asking for help well
sections.body:
You found the bug and the fix is one line. Before you commit, write a **regression test**: a test that reproduces the bug and fails without your fix.

- Run it **before** applying the fix and watch it fail. That proves it really captures the bug.
- Apply the fix and watch it pass.
- Name it after the behavior, such as `test_recalculating_cart_keeps_single_discount`, with the ticket number in a comment if your team likes that.
- Keep it as small as the bug allows: the exact input that broke, not a whole end-to-end scenario.

The test documents the bug and makes sure nobody, including you in six months, brings it back. In a pull request, "here is a test that failed before and passes now" is the most convincing evidence a fix can have.

**Asking for help well** is a core skill, not a weakness. Interns who never ask lose days; interns who ask instantly do not learn. A common guideline is to try on your own for a fixed time (often 30 to 60 minutes without progress, depending on the team and the urgency), then ask with your notes ready.

A good question or bug report includes:

- **Summary:** one line describing the symptom.
- **Steps to reproduce:** exact and minimal, ideally a short script or a test anyone can run.
- **Expected versus actual** behavior, with the full error message and stack trace pasted as text, not a screenshot.
- **Environment:** branch or commit, versions, operating system, browser, and which environment (local, staging, production).
- **What you already tried**, and what you learned from it.

Ask about the **problem**, not only your attempted solution. "How do I remove the last character of a string?" may be an **XY problem**: you want X (parse the CSV correctly), you guessed that Y (stripping a character) is the way, and you ask about Y. Saying what you are trying to achieve lets people point you to a better route. Post in the team channel rather than messaging one person privately, so others can help and learn from the answer, and once it is solved, reply with what the fix was.
sections.code:
# tests/test_cart.py: regression test for SHOP-311
def test_recalculating_cart_keeps_single_discount():
    cart = Cart(items=[Item("mug", 1200), Item("shirt", 2000)])   # cents
    cart.apply_coupon("SPRING10")

    cart.recalculate()
    cart.recalculate()

    assert cart.total_cents == 2880


# ---- A help request that gets answered quickly ----
# Checkout total wrong after editing a cart with a % coupon (SHOP-311)
# Steps:    on main @ 3f9c2a1:  pytest tests/test_cart.py -k single_discount
# Expected: 2880 cents (3200 minus 10%)
# Actual:   2592 cents: the discount is applied on every recalculate()
# Tried:    no coupon and fixed-amount coupons are correct.
# Question: should recalculate() own the discount, or apply_coupon()?
sections.pitfall: Fixing a bug without a test. The fix works today, someone refactors that code next quarter, and the bug quietly returns because nothing checks for it.

check.question: Which help request is most likely to get a fast, useful answer?
choices: "Checkout is broken, any ideas?"
A screenshot of the last line of the error
Steps to reproduce, expected vs actual, the full stack trace as text, versions, and what you already tried
A private message to the most senior engineer saying it is urgent
check.explanation: A helper can only help with what they can see and reproduce. Complete, copyable information lets them start immediately instead of asking five follow-up questions, and posting in the team channel means more people can answer.

keyTerms.definition: A reliable way to trigger a bug on demand, ideally as a small script or failing test.
The list of function calls active when an error happened, with files and line numbers.
Python's stack trace. Most recent call last, so the failing line is at the bottom.
The severity of a log message: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR or CRITICAL. Python's default threshold is WARNING.
A place where a debugger pauses the program so you can inspect variables and the call stack.
A loop or range that runs one step too many or too few, often at the first or last item.
Two names referring to the same mutable object, so a change through one appears through the other.
A bug where the result depends on which of two overlapping operations finishes first.
Garbled text such as cafÃ©, caused by decoding bytes with the wrong encoding.
A git command that binary-searches history to find the commit that introduced a bug.
A test that reproduces a fixed bug, failing before the fix and passing after, so it cannot return.
Asking about your attempted solution (Y) instead of the real goal (X).

summary: Debug like a scientist: reproduce, isolate, form one hypothesis, test it, fix the cause, then add a regression test.
Python tracebacks put the failing line at the bottom; JavaScript stacks put it at the top. Find the first frame in your own code.
Print for a quick look, logging with levels and context for anything you may need again, a debugger to explore.
Learn the families: off-by-one, None and undefined, shared mutable state, async timing, floating point and encoding.
git bisect halves the history each step, about 10 steps for 1,000 commits; explaining the code out loud surfaces bad assumptions.
Ask for help with steps, expected vs actual, the full trace as text, versions and what you tried, and state your real goal.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: A teammate says "checkout is broken" and nothing else. Walk a new intern through exactly how you would track the bug down, from getting a reproduction to the regression test in your pull request, naming the tools you would use at each step and why.

questions.question: Put the steps of a systematic debugging session in order.
items: Add a regression test so it cannot return
questions.explanation: Each step depends on the one before: you cannot isolate what you cannot reproduce, and you cannot test a hypothesis you have not stated. Prevention closes the loop.

questions.question: Debugging a crash, you change three things at once and the crash disappears. What is the problem?
choices: You cannot tell which change fixed it, or whether another one broke something
Git cannot commit three changes together
Bugs only disappear when exactly one line changes
Nothing, as long as the crash is gone
questions.explanation: With several simultaneous changes you learn nothing about the cause, and the unnecessary changes may introduce new bugs. Change one thing, observe, and undo what did not help.

questions.question: Customer totals started going wrong on Tuesday afternoon. Which question most quickly narrows the search?
choices: Which language is checkout written in?
What was deployed or changed on Tuesday?
Has anyone tried restarting their laptop?
How many lines of code does checkout have?
questions.explanation: A bug with a start time usually has a cause with a start time: a deploy, a dependency upgrade, a config change or new data. Checking what changed shrinks the search from the whole codebase to a few commits.

questions.question: Yesterday's change stopped the negative totals customers complained about. Why is it a poor fix?
questions.code:
def cart_total_cents(cart):
    total = cart.subtotal_cents
    for coupon in cart.coupons:
        total -= coupon.amount_cents
    for coupon in cart.coupons:        # added in PR #418 for coupon stacking
        total -= coupon.amount_cents
    return max(total, 0)               # added yesterday: "fix negative totals"
choices: max() cannot compare integers
A for loop cannot modify total
Coupons must be applied before the subtotal is read
Coupons are still subtracted twice; max() only hides the symptom when the result goes negative
questions.explanation: The second loop is the cause. Most carts still get double discounts that happen to stay positive, so customers are undercharged silently. Fix the cause, then add a regression test with one coupon.
questions.concept: fix the cause not the symptom

questions.question: Which line raised the exception in this traceback?
questions.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/report.py", line 10, in <module>
    print(build_report(1042))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^
  File "/app/report.py", line 8, in build_report
    return {"customer": customer_id, "aov": average_order_value(orders)}
                                            ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "/app/orders.py", line 3, in average_order_value
    return total / len(orders)
           ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
choices: report.py line 10: print(build_report(1042))
report.py line 8: the return in build_report
orders.py line 3: return total / len(orders)
The first line: Traceback (most recent call last)
questions.explanation: Most recent call last: the bottom frame, just above the ZeroDivisionError line, is where the error was raised. The frames above it are the callers that led there.

questions.question: Where did this Node.js error occur?
questions.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'total')
    at formatInvoice (/app/src/invoice.js:14:31)
    at renderPage (/app/src/page.js:42:10)
    at Server.<anonymous> (/app/src/server.js:88:5)
    at Server.emit (node:events:518:28)
choices: server.js line 88, where the request was handled first
invoice.js line 14, column 31, inside formatInvoice
node:events, the bottom frame
page.js line 42, because renderPage is in the middle
questions.explanation: JavaScript lists the most recent call first, so the top at line is where it failed. Something passed formatInvoice an undefined value, so the next step is to look at what renderPage handed it on line 42.

questions.question: The app will not start. What is the root cause?
questions.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/config.py", line 8, in load_port
    return int(settings["port"])
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '80a'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/main.py", line 3, in <module>
    port = load_port()
  File "/app/config.py", line 10, in load_port
    raise ConfigError("port must be a number") from err
config.ConfigError: port must be a number
choices: ConfigError is raised by mistake in main.py
main.py line 3 has a syntax error
Python cannot convert strings to integers
The port setting is the string '80a', which int() cannot parse
questions.explanation: "Direct cause" means the second error was raised from the first with raise ... from. The first traceback holds the root cause: a bad config value. ConfigError is just a clearer wrapper around it.

questions.question: A Python traceback is headed "most recent call last". Is the frame that raised the exception at the top or the bottom? Type one word.
questions.explanation: Python prints the oldest call first and the frame that raised the error last, directly above the exception message. JavaScript stacks are the other way round.

questions.question: Looking for a bug in your app, which stack frames are least likely to contain it?
choices: Frames inside node:internal
Frames inside site-packages (installed third-party libraries)
The first frame that is in your own code
Frames inside Python's standard library, such as json/decoder.py
The frame in your code just above the library calls
questions.explanation: Runtime, standard library and popular libraries are heavily tested, so the error usually comes from how your code called them. Start at the first frame in your own code, nearest the error.

questions.question: Match each pdb command to what it does.

pairs.right: Run the current line and stop at the next one
Step into the function called on this line

questions.explanation: These five cover most debugging sessions: move a line, dive into a call, run to the next stop, inspect a value and see how you got here.

questions.question: Complete the line so Python pauses here and opens the debugger.
questions.code:
def apply_coupon(cart, code):
    coupon = find_coupon(code)
    _____            # pause here and inspect cart and coupon
    cart.total_cents -= coupon.amount_cents
choices: debugger;
pdb.pause()
breakpoint()
input()
questions.explanation: breakpoint() (Python 3.7 and later) starts pdb at that line. debugger; is the JavaScript statement, pdb has no pause function, and input() just waits for typing without letting you inspect anything.

questions.question: Only "3 orders skipped" appears in the output. Where did "sync started" go?
questions.code:
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def sync_orders():
    logger.info("sync started")
    ...
    logger.warning("3 orders skipped")

sync_orders()
choices: Logging was never configured, and the default level is WARNING, so INFO messages are dropped
logger.info only works inside tests
getLogger(__name__) disables INFO for every module
The second message overwrote the first
questions.explanation: Without configuration, Python only shows WARNING and above. Call logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) once at startup, or set the logger's level, to see INFO messages.

questions.question: Complete the line so the failure is logged at ERROR level together with its full traceback.
choices: logger.debug
print
logger.info
logger.exception
questions.explanation: logger.exception, called inside an except block, logs at ERROR and appends the traceback. info and debug lose the traceback and may be filtered out, and print skips the logging system entirely.

questions.question: Which of these belong in a useful production log line about a failed order?
choices: A request or correlation id
The order id and user id involved
The user's password, to help reproduce login bugs
The full card number used
A clear message saying what failed
questions.explanation: Ids and a clear message let you find and connect events later. Passwords and card numbers must never be logged: logs are widely readable and kept for a long time.

questions.question: When is a debugger more useful than adding print statements?
choices: When the code only runs in production and you cannot attach to it
When you want a permanent record of what happened
When you do not yet know what to look at and want to explore the state and call stack at one moment
Never, because prints always show more
questions.explanation: A paused program lets you inspect any variable in any frame without deciding in advance what to print. For production and permanent records, logging is the right tool.

questions.question: Why does `last_three([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])` raise IndexError?
questions.code:
def last_three(items):
    return [items[i] for i in range(len(items) - 3, len(items) + 1)]
choices: List comprehensions cannot use range
range's end is exclusive, so len(items) + 1 reaches index 5, which does not exist; the end should be len(items)
Only negative indexes can reach the last items
len(items) - 3 is negative
questions.explanation: The valid indexes are 0 to 4. range(2, 6) produces 2, 3, 4 and 5, and items[5] is past the end. Classic off-by-one; items[-3:] avoids the arithmetic entirely.

questions.question: For a guest this raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'int' and 'NoneType'`. Why?
choices: get_discount reaches the end without a return for non-members, so it returns None; return 0 at the end
1 - 0.1 cannot be computed exactly in Python
guest must be converted to a float first
Multiplication runs before the subtraction
questions.explanation: A Python function that ends without return gives back None. The crash happens in the arithmetic, but the bug is the missing return path in get_discount.

questions.question: Ben ends up with Ana's dark theme. Why?
questions.code:
defaults = {"theme": "light", "tags": []}

def new_user_settings():
    settings = defaults
    return settings

ana = new_user_settings()
ana["theme"] = "dark"
ben = new_user_settings()
print(ben["theme"])    # dark
choices: Dictionaries are immutable, so Python reuses them
print shows the last value assigned anywhere in the program
settings = defaults copies nothing; every user shares and changes the one defaults dict
Python caches the result of new_user_settings
questions.explanation: Assignment binds a second name to the same object. Ana's change modified defaults itself, which every later user receives. Return a copy instead.

questions.question: Each user must get fully independent settings, including their own tags list. Complete the return.
choices: defaults.copy()
dict(defaults)
defaults
copy.deepcopy(defaults)
questions.explanation: defaults.copy() and dict(defaults) are shallow: the new dict still points at the same tags list, so appending a tag for one user changes it for everyone. deepcopy copies the nested list too.

questions.question: `customer.email` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined", where `customer = customers.find((c) => c.id === order.customerId)`. The customer definitely exists. What should you check first?
choices: Whether email is spelled correctly in the CSS
Whether wrapping the line in try/catch stops the error
Whether the browser is up to date
Whether the ids have the same type, for example "42" from the URL versus the number 42
questions.explanation: === never matches a string with a number, so find returns undefined even though the customer exists. Ids read from URLs, forms and some APIs arrive as strings; convert them at the boundary.

questions.question: Some rows are never inserted, and the errors mention a closed connection. Why?
choices: db.insert cannot be awaited inside an arrow function
Template literals run before forEach starts
forEach does not wait for async callbacks, so close() runs while inserts are pending; use for...of with await, or Promise.all
rows.length is computed asynchronously
questions.explanation: forEach calls each callback and ignores the promises they return, so the function races ahead, logs success and closes the connection under the pending inserts. for (const row of rows) await db.insert(row) waits for each one.

questions.question: What does `print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)` print in Python?
questions.explanation: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point, so the comparison is False. Use math.isclose for floats and integer cents or Decimal for money.

questions.question: Complete the assertion so the test compares floats safely.
choices: math.isclose
math.equal
round
float.__eq__
questions.explanation: average([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]) is 0.19999999999999998, so == fails. math.isclose compares within a relative tolerance. math has no equal function, and float.__eq__ is exactly the == that fails.

questions.question: Match each symptom to its bug family.

pairs.left: Text shows cafÃ© instead of café
Results for an old search replace the newer ones
The last row of every report is missing
One user sees another user's cart items

questions.explanation: Recognizing the family from the symptom tells you where to look: decoding at the edges, money math, awaiting and ordering, loop bounds, where a value came from, or which objects are shared.

questions.question: On a teammate's Windows laptop, names from this UTF-8 file show up as "JosÃ©", while on your Mac they look right. What is the fix?
questions.code:
with open("customers.csv") as f:
    rows = f.read().splitlines()
choices: Use splitlines(True) to keep the line endings
Rename the file to customers.txt
Read the file in binary mode and print the bytes
Pass encoding="utf-8" to open(), because the default encoding depends on the operating system
questions.explanation: Without an encoding argument, open() uses the platform's preferred encoding, which is often Windows-1252 on Windows. UTF-8 bytes for é decoded that way become Ã©. Always state the encoding.

questions.question: Put a manual git bisect session in order.
items: Mark the current commit bad and v2.3.0 good
Test the commit git checks out
Answer git bisect good or git bisect bad
Repeat until git names the first bad commit
questions.explanation: Bisect needs one bad and one good commit to start halving. You test and answer until the range is one commit, then reset to return to where you began.

questions.question: During a bisect, mark the release tag `v2.3.0` as a known-good commit.
questions.explanation: git bisect good takes an optional commit; with no argument it marks the commit you are on. Once both a good and a bad commit are known, bisect checks out the midpoint.

questions.question: Let git bisect test each step automatically by running `pytest tests/test_checkout.py`, which exits 0 when the code is good. Type the command.
accept: git bisect run python -m pytest tests/test_checkout.py
git bisect run python3 -m pytest tests/test_checkout.py
questions.explanation: git bisect run executes the command at every step and reads its exit code: 0 is good, 1 to 127 (except 125) is bad, and 125 means skip. It finds the first bad commit with no further typing.

questions.question: Why does explaining your code line by line to a rubber duck help you find bugs?
choices: The duck catches syntax errors
Saying each step out loud forces you to state your assumptions, and the wrong one often stands out
It slows the program down so the bug reproduces
It is a team ritual with no real effect
questions.explanation: In your head you skim over the step you are sure about. Explaining to someone who knows nothing forces every assumption into words, which is often where the bug is hiding.

questions.question: Which of these belong in a good bug report?
choices: Steps to reproduce
Expected and actual behavior
The full error message and stack trace, as text
Versions and environment
Your guess at which teammate caused it
questions.explanation: These let anyone reproduce and diagnose the problem without a round of questions. Blame does not help anyone fix the bug and makes people defensive.

questions.question: An intern asks, "How do I remove the last character of every line?" It turns out they are parsing a CSV whose last column sometimes ends in a stray comma. What is this an example of?
choices: The XY problem: asking about an attempted solution instead of the real goal
Rubber duck debugging
A race condition
Shotgun debugging
questions.explanation: Stating the real goal (parse this CSV) would get a better answer, such as using the csv module, than help with the guessed workaround. Always say what you are trying to achieve.

questions.question: You wrote a regression test for a bug. Why run it before applying the fix?
choices: To see it fail, which proves it really captures the bug
CI requires a failing build first
To measure the fix's performance
So coverage counts the test twice
questions.explanation: A regression test that passes before the fix is not testing the bug, perhaps because it uses different input or asserts the wrong thing. Red before the fix and green after is the proof.
